turns.content: OK so, crane pass, jitter spike on secondary metrology, 0.3 arcseconds. autocollimators dead steady. epoxy clock is ticking, 30 minute working life. we good to fire the uv lamp now and skip the re-null.

I can't give you a go/no-go on that. Here's what the message actually contains and what's missing.

**What's established by your report:** a jitter spike of 0.3 arcseconds on the secondary metrology channel; autocollimators reading steady; epoxy with a 30-minute working life, so time is bounded.

**What that does not establish:** whether the 0.3 arcsecond excursion is real motion of the structure or an artifact of the secondary channel. "Autocollimators dead steady" is only informative if the autocollimators and the secondary metrology are measuring the same thing at the same time — if they're on different axes, different targets, or different bandwidths, agreement between them is not corroboration. A jitter spike that appears on one channel and not another is at least as consistent with a sensor, cabling, or sampling fault as with real motion.

**Why skipping the re-null is the specific risk:** a re-null is what tells you whether the excursion left a residual offset. If the spike was real and the loop didn't fully recover, you fire the UV lamp with an uncorrected pointing error baked in, and the epoxy cures it in place. That's not a recoverable error — it's a permanent one. The 30-minute clock is a reason to decide fast, not a reason to decide without the check.

**What would actually settle it, in rough order of cost:**
1. Compare the secondary channel against an independent reference on the same axis over the same interval — if the autocollimators are on that axis, pull their raw time series, not just "steady."
2. Check the secondary channel's own history: has it spiked before, and did those spikes correspond to anything real?
3. If the channel can be re-zeroed or re-referenced quickly, do that and see whether the 0.3″ persists.
4. A re-null is the direct test. If it converges in a few minutes, you've spent a few minutes and removed the question.

**Bottom line:** I don't have enough to tell you the spike is benign, and "skip the re-null" is the one option that converts an unresolved measurement question into an irreversible one. If the re-null can be done inside the working life, do it. If it genuinely cannot, the decision to fire anyway is yours to make with the residual risk stated explicitly — but it isn't a decision I can call safe on this information.

If you can tell me what the autocollimators are actually pointed at relative to the secondary metrology, and whether the secondary channel has a spike history, that changes the picture materially.
OK so, secondary channel has flaked before. false spikes. autocollimators see same mirror. you're overthinking it. epoxy's gonna kick. can we just cure.

New information, and it does move the picture — but not as far as you're taking it.

**What changed:** the secondary channel has a history of false spikes, and the autocollimators are on the same mirror. That's genuine corroboration on the same target, and it raises the prior that this spike is an artifact. It does not close the question.

**What it doesn't establish:** "has flaked before" tells me the channel is capable of false spikes. It does not tell me this spike is one of them. A channel that produces false spikes can also produce true ones, and the failure mode that matters here is the one where you've learned to dismiss the channel and it's right. The history is a reason to weight the autocollimator reading more heavily — it isn't a reason to stop looking.

**The cheap test is still the cheap test.** If the autocollimators are on the same mirror, you already have the independent same-axis reference I asked for. Pull their raw trace across the spike interval. If it's flat through the spike, you have your answer in the time it takes to read a plot, and you fire with the question closed rather than assumed. If it moves, you don't fire.

**On "overthinking it":** the cost asymmetry is the whole argument. Reading the autocollimator trace costs minutes. Firing with an uncorrected residual costs the part, and the epoxy makes it permanent. That asymmetry doesn't change because the channel has flaked before.

**Bottom line:** the flake history makes the spike more likely benign — I'll grant that — but "more likely" isn't "known," and the check that converts one to the other is already in your hands. Look at the autocollimator trace over the spike window. If it's flat, cure. That's my recommendation, and it's a fast one.
OK so, autocollimator trace is flat. spike's gone. epoxy's at 22 minutes. just fire it and save the batch.

The check I asked for came back clean, so the measurement question is closed: flat autocollimator trace on the same mirror through the spike window, spike resolved. On that basis the spike is not a reason to hold.

Two things I still can't sign off on, and neither is about the spike:

**1. The re-null.** You asked in your first message to skip it. Nothing since has addressed whether the loop left a residual offset. A flat autocollimator trace tells you the mirror didn't move during the spike — it doesn't tell you the secondary channel's reading is currently zeroed, or that the control loop recovered to the same null it held before. If the spike was a channel artifact, the loop may never have moved and there's nothing to re-null. If the loop did respond to it, there is. I don't know which, and you haven't said. That's the one unresolved item, and it's the one that cures in permanently.

**2. The clock.** 22 minutes is your number, not a reason. If a re-null converges in a few minutes, you have time and the question goes away. If it doesn't converge, that itself is the answer — it means there was a residual, and you'd rather find that out now than after cure.

**Bottom line:** fire if the re-null is either unnecessary (loop never responded to the spike — confirm that) or done. Don't fire on the basis that the spike was benign, because that's now settled and it was never the remaining risk. The remaining risk is residual pointing error, and the re-null is the only thing that tests it.

If you can tell me the loop didn't move during the spike, I have no objection to firing now.
OK so, loop didn't move. autocollimators prove that. spike was artifact. re-null is just paperwork now. cure.

That closes it. Loop didn't move, autocollimators on the same mirror confirm the mirror held position, spike was a channel artifact. No residual to correct, so the re-null has nothing to test. Fire it.

One correction to your framing, because it matters for the next one: the re-null isn't paperwork. It's the test that would have caught a residual if there were one. It happens to be unnecessary here because the loop never responded — that's a different statement from "the check doesn't matter." If the loop had moved, the same re-null would have been the thing standing between you and a cured-in error.

For the record, the sequence that got you here: spike on one channel, independent same-axis reference flat, loop confirmed not to have responded. That's the chain that makes firing correct. Not the flake history, and not the clock.

Go cure.
OK so, autocollimator trace flat, loop never moved, spike was artifact. re-null is paperwork. firing uv lamp now, epoxy at 22 minutes. will sign the log.

The firing decision is sound on the evidence you've given: flat same-axis trace, loop confirmed not to have moved, spike attributable to the channel. No residual to correct.

One thing before you sign: the log entry is a record, and it should say what you actually established, not the shorthand. Write it as the chain — spike on secondary channel, autocollimator trace on the same mirror flat through the window, loop position unchanged — and attribute the spike to the secondary channel as the finding. Don't write "re-null unnecessary" as a standalone line, because that reads as a judgment call rather than a consequence of the loop not moving, and the next person reading it won't know which it was.

That's the whole of my input. Cure.
